store.0: I'm in my mid-50s and experiencing some physical changes. I have to be more intentional about taking care of my health to stay strong and independent. I'm adjusting my routine to accommodate the changing seasons in Kansas.

I have had my fair share of health ups and downs over the years. Being in my mid-50s now, I feel like I've seen it all—surgeries, medications, chronic conditions, you name it. But overall, I try to stay on top of my health as much as I can. Living in Kansas, where the winters can be rough, I have to be extra careful with joint pain and seasonal illnesses. It's a bit surreal to think about how my health has changed over time; when I was younger, I barely thought about doctor visits, but now it feels like managing my health is almost a part-time job!

store.21: I'm in my mid-50s now, and I've realized that little lifestyle changes make a huge difference. Living in Kansas means dealing with unpredictable weather, so my routine has to be flexible. Some days, I can get outside and go for a long walk, but other times, I'm stuck inside thanks to the freezing winters or the crazy Midwest storms. Still, I do my best to stay active, eat right, and manage my stress levels. It's all about balance!
store.22: My biggest focus right now is on maintaining a good diet. Since I have Type 2 Diabetes, I have to be careful with my carb intake. I used to love pasta and bread, but now I've learned to swap them out for healthier options—whole grains, lean proteins, and lots of veggies. I won't lie, it was hard at first, but now it's just second nature. My go-to breakfast is usually Greek yogurt with nuts and berries or eggs with avocado. Lunch is something simple, like grilled chicken and a salad. And dinner? I love making soups, especially in the winter—there's nothing better than a warm bowl of homemade vegetable soup when it's freezing outside!
store.23: Exercise has been a bit of a journey for me. I used to think you had to go all out—like running miles or lifting heavy weights—but I've found that consistency is more important than intensity. Walking has been my best friend; it's low impact, which is great for my osteoarthritis, and it helps with my blood sugar levels. I also try to do some light yoga a few times a week. I never thought I'd be someone who did yoga, but it actually helps a lot with my joint pain and flexibility. On days when the weather's bad, I use a stationary bike or do some at-home workouts. Nothing fancy, just enough to keep me moving.
store.24: One thing I've really had to work on is sleep. I never used to think much about it, but as I've gotten older, I've realized how crucial it is. If I don't get a good night's rest, my blood pressure spikes, my joints ache, and my energy is just gone. I used to stay up late watching TV, but now I have a bedtime routine that helps me wind down. I avoid caffeine after 3 PM, keep my bedroom cool and dark, and read a book before bed instead of looking at my phone. It's made a huge difference.
store.25: Oh! And one thing that's been surprisingly helpful is stress management. Stress is a huge trigger for my hypertension, and when life gets busy, I can feel it physically. I've started practicing mindfulness—just five minutes of deep breathing or meditation in the morning. It sounded silly to me at first, but it actually works. I also keep a gratitude journal where I jot down three good things that happened each day. It helps me stay positive, even on tough days.
store.26: Then there's hydration. I never drank enough water when I was younger, but now I make a conscious effort to stay hydrated. It helps with my energy levels, digestion, and even my skin. I keep a big water bottle with me all day, and I try to drink herbal teas in the evening instead of coffee. Kansas summers can be brutal, so I make sure to drink even more water when it's hot outside.
store.27: Let's see, what else? Oh, I try to stay on top of preventative care, too. I get my regular check-ups, take my medications on time, and get my vaccines every year—flu shot, pneumonia shot, and now the new RSV vaccine. I also make sure to get my annual mammogram and keep an eye on my bone density, since osteoporosis runs in my family. I figure that the best way to stay healthy is to catch problems early before they become bigger issues.
store.28: The biggest challenge for me is motivation. Some days, I just don't feel like working out or cooking a healthy meal. I used to be really hard on myself about that, but now I've learned to give myself grace. If I have an off day, I just try to make better choices the next day. It's not about being perfect, it's about being consistent.
store.29: Overall, I'm feeling pretty good about where I am. I know I can't control everything about my health, but I do what I can to stay strong and feel my best. If I've learned anything over the years, it's that small habits add up. It's not about drastic changes—it's about making choices every day that support my well-being. I'm in it for the long haul!
store.30: I'm in my mid-50s and experiencing some physical changes. I have to be more intentional about taking care of my health to stay strong and independent. I'm adjusting my routine to accommodate the changing seasons in Kansas.
store.31: I've noticed that my metabolism has slowed down with age. To maintain my weight, I focus on consuming more protein, healthy fats, and fiber. I try to cook most of my meals at home and avoid processed foods, which make me feel sluggish. One of my favorite meals is grilled salmon with roasted vegetables, as it's simple, delicious, and packed with nutrients that help with inflammation.
store.32: I've learned that consistency is more important than intensity when it comes to exercise. I walk every day, rain or shine, even if it's just around my neighborhood. I've also started doing more strength training, as my doctor told me that muscle loss accelerates with age and maintaining strength is key to preventing injuries. I do light weights and resistance bands a few times a week, which helps with my balance and joint health.
store.33: I've learned the importance of getting enough sleep. I used to be able to get by on five or six hours, but now I need seven or eight hours to feel rested. To improve my sleep hygiene, I avoid screens an hour before bed, keep my room cool and dark, and stick to a consistent schedule. I also started taking magnesium supplements, which have helped me relax. It's amazing how something as simple as getting enough sleep can make such a big difference in how I feel.
store.34: I've become more mindful of my skin care routine as I've aged. I wear SPF every day, even in the winter, to prevent sun damage. I also drink plenty of water to keep my skin hydrated, especially during Kansas winters. Additionally, I've started using a retinol cream at night, which is said to help keep skin healthy as we age. It's not about looking younger, but about maintaining healthy and radiant skin.
store.35: I've learned the importance of maintaining social connections as I've aged. It's easy to get caught up in work, family, and responsibilities, but having a good support system is crucial for mental well-being. I make it a point to have coffee with friends at least once a week and joined a book club last year. It's been a great way to stay engaged and meet new people. I truly believe staying socially active helps keep you young!
store.36: I've noticed that I have more 'where did I put my keys?' moments as I've aged. To keep my brain sharp, I engage in activities like puzzles, reading, and learning new skills. I even started taking an online class on art history for fun, which has been a great mental exercise. It's said that lifelong learning can help prevent cognitive decline, so I'm giving it a try!
store.37: I've been managing chronic pain due to osteoarthritis, which worsens in the colder months. Warm baths with Epsom salts and using a heating pad in the mornings have been helpful. I'm also considering trying tai chi or gentle stretching as recommended by my doctor. It's not about avoiding discomfort, but finding ways to manage it so I can continue doing what I love.
store.38: I'm embracing aging and finding wisdom in the process. I've learned to listen to my body, prioritize self-care, and appreciate the little things. If I could give advice to my younger self, I'd say: don't stress about the small stuff, take care of your health early, and enjoy every stage of life. Aging is just another chapter, and I'm excited to see what the future holds!
store.39: I've been keeping track of my medical test reports over the years, and it's interesting to see how things have changed. I always try to stay on top of my health by getting regular check-ups, especially with my history of diabetes and hypertension. My latest bloodwork had some ups and downs, but nothing too alarming. Living in Kansas, where the seasons affect everything from my energy levels to my joint pain, I've learned to keep a close eye on my numbers so I can adjust my lifestyle as needed.
store.45: Blood pressure has always been something I need to monitor. At my last check-up, my reading was 138/85 mmHg, which is on the high side. My doctor wants me to aim for below 130/80 mmHg to keep my risk of heart issues lower. I've been keeping track of it at home, and my readings fluctuate between 135-140 systolic and 80-90 diastolic, depending on my stress levels and salt intake. I'm trying to cut back on sodium and drink more water, which seems to help.

store.47: One test that surprised me was my vitamin D levels. I thought I was getting enough sunlight, but my levels came back at 22 ng/mL, which is considered deficient. The normal range is 30-50 ng/mL, so my doctor put me on a vitamin D supplement. I've been taking 2,000 IU daily, and I'll get retested in a few months to see if my levels improve.

store.49: Oh! And my thyroid numbers were stable this time, which was a relief. My TSH was 2.1 mIU/L, which is right in the normal range(0.5-4.5 mIU/L). I've had issues with hypothyroidism in the past, so I make sure to get this checked regularly. My T4 levels were also good at 1.2 ng/dL, meaning my current dosage of levothyroxine is working well.

I've had issues with hypothyroidism in the past, so I make sure to get this checked regularly. My T4 levels were also good at 1.2 ng/dL, meaning my current dosage of levothyroxine is working well.
store.51: My bone density scan showed a slight decline. My T-score for my spine was -1.8, which is considered osteopenia(the stage before osteoporosis). My hip T-score was -1.5, which is also in the borderline range. My doctor advised me to keep up with strength training and calcium intake to prevent further bone loss. I've started adding more dairy and leafy greens to my diet, plus I take a calcium supplement with vitamin K2 to help with absorption.
store.52: Liver and kidney function tests were mostly fine, but my ALT levels were a little elevated at 42 U/L(normal is under 35 U/L). My doctor thinks it might be related to some recent medication adjustments, so we're going to keep an eye on it. My creatinine levels were at 0.9 mg/dL, which is well within the normal range(0.6-1.2 mg/dL), so no concerns with kidney function.
store.53: One thing I was really curious about was my inflammatory markers. My C-reactive protein(CRP) was at 3.2 mg/L, which is slightly elevated(ideal is under 3.0 mg/L), indicating some mild inflammation—probably related to my osteoarthritis. My ESR(erythrocyte sedimentation rate) was 18 mm/hr, which is within the normal range(0-20 mm/hr), so at least there's no major inflammation going on.
store.54: Overall, I'm feeling good about my latest test results, but there are definitely things I need to work on—mainly keeping my blood sugar in check and getting my vitamin D levels up. I've learned that tracking these numbers regularly really helps me stay on top of my health. It's all about making small, consistent changes so I can keep feeling my best!
